blocks.x: Spend five minutes on FitTok and you’d think longevity requires a cold plunge at dawn, peptides aplenty, and enough weekly training volume to qualify as a Navy SEAL. The reality, however, is less dramatic. If you want to live longer, recent research from Harvard offers a surprisingly reassuring message: Your lifting routine is probably a lot closer to the ideal for longevity than your algorithm would lead you to believe.

Published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, this study compiled data from three cohorts of nearly 150,000 adults—most of them middle-aged—spanning 30 years. Compared to people who didn’t lift at all, those who logged 90 to 120 minutes a week saw the biggest longevity payoff: a 13% lower risk of death from any cause, a 19% lower risk of cardiovascular death, and a 27% lower risk of death from neurological diseases. That’s just three or four half-hour workouts, or even two 45-minute sessions. Perhaps surprisingly, anything more than that didn’t appear to move the needle. After about two hours a week, the longevity perks plateaued.
The strength training and longevity connection

Your muscles do a lot more than help you PR your deadlift or make your sleeves fit tighter. “Muscle is not just structural tissue; it is your body’s largest endocrine organ,” says Vonda Wright, MD, an orthopedic surgeon and the creator of Skeletal Longevity. “Every time you contract a muscle against resistance, it releases signaling molecules called myokines that travel through your bloodstream and reduce systemic inflammation—the root cause of virtually every chronic disease of aging.” You can also expect better blood sugar control, stronger bones, improved metabolic health, and then some.

Plus, resistance training protects against the gradual loss of strength and independence that tends to accompany aging. “It allows us to interact with our environment more consistently, more comfortably, and more capably,” adds Alex Rothstein, EdD, MS, CSCS, exercise physiologist and coordinator of the exercise Science program at New York Institute of Technology.

As for those cardiovascular benefits? The study results might be surprising since we tend to think that protecting your heart requires running on a treadmill or swimming laps. Yet according to Dr. Wright, long-term resistance training remodels the vascular system, making arteries more elastic and compliant. This ultimately helps to manage blood pressure and reduce heart attack risk. “It also reduces visceral fat: the dangerous inflammatory fat that wraps around your organs and drives cardiovascular disease,” she adds.

Meanwhile, Dr. Wright says that strength training may also protect the brain because working muscles release compounds that stimulate the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Experts call this protein Miracle-Gro for your brain since it helps neurons grow and communicate more effectively.

It’s not news that lifting weights can help you live a longer, healthier life. What is, however, is how little it appears to take. If you already lift on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday for a half-hour after work, consider this a permission slip to stop confusing ‘more’ with ‘better.’ According to this study, your ROI starts shrinking beyond the 90-to-120 minute range.

But before you watch the clock like a hawk, you should think of the range as a useful benchmark rather than a prescription. Even the researchers advise interpreting the results with a grain of salt. “Importantly, 90 to 120 minutes should not be interpreted as a strict target or threshold, given we did not have data on specific types of resistance training, intensity, and number of sets,” say study co-authors Yiwen Zhang, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow and Edward Giovannucci, MD, professor of nutrition and epidemiology, both at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Future research is necessary to dial in on these parameters. Nonetheless, there are a few things you can keep in mind when building out your own workout routine to promote longevity.

Per Zhang and Dr. Giovannucci, the research focused primarily on free weights and resistance machines. While it’s smart to continue lifting heavy, Rothstein says you shouldn’t necessarily sleep on bodyweight exercises. “I’m a big fan since they’re very transferable to everyone’s daily life,” he says. Just be sure there’s enough stimulus to promote physiological adaptation. And no matter which types of resistance training make it into your routine, consistency and adherence over the long run are key.

In addition, Dr. Wright cautions against confusing muscle size with the kind of strength that promotes healthy aging. From a longevity standpoint, she says that functional strength—the ability to carry groceries, get up off the floor, or catch yourself before a fall—is ultimately more valuable than chasing bigger biceps.

Last but not least: as important as strength training is, don’t pass up on cardio either. In fact, the study found that participants who paired aerobics and strength training yielded the most benefit, with a 45% lower risk of mortality than those who did neither.

“The clearest message is to include both aerobic activity and resistance training as part of a long-term routine,” say Zhang and Dr. Giovannucci. Rothstein gives the green light to aim for 90 to 120 minutes of strength training per week—portioning it out as it fits your schedule—but also clocking in about 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise. The pairing, he says, will “give you the best of both worlds and really influence not only your longevity but also your quality of life.”
